source_text: Et quamvis iam pro concupiscentia vel voluptate carnis, quae etiam libido dicitur, quae sexibus ob virilitatem propagationis inserta est, primo illo opusculo eatenus disputaverim, ut docerem illam nihil aliud esse quam unam de instrumentis corporis rationabilibus et irrationabilibus aeque inditam ad Dei operam pertinentem, qui carnem nostram in sensibus affecisset, tamen, quia ei vehementer Augustinus incumbit eamque dicit malam, id est peccatum esse naturale atque omnium peccatorum parentem, quod pudore eius potissimum persuadere conatur meque irridet, qui eam erubescam nominare directim.
pass_a_gloss: And although already for the desire or pleasure of the flesh, which is also called lust, which has been inserted in the sexes for the virility of propagation, I had disputed in that first little work to such an extent that I would teach that it is nothing other than one of the rational and irrational instruments of the body equally implanted, pertaining to the work of God, who had affected our flesh in the senses, nevertheless, because Augustine vehemently leans on it and says it is evil, that is that sin is natural and the parent of all sins, which he tries to persuade especially by the shame of it and mocks me, who am ashamed to name it directly.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS libido; Blaise often sexual desire; Julian treats as created sensation, not a sin-nature
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: In that first work I had already argued about fleshly desire or pleasure, also called lust, implanted in the sexes for the reproductive activity of generation. I showed that it is nothing other than one of the body’s instruments, implanted alike in rational and irrational beings and belonging to God’s work, since he equipped our flesh with sensations. Yet Augustine attacks it fiercely, calling it evil—that is, natural sin and the parent of every sin. He tries to persuade us chiefly from its shame, and mocks me for being ashamed to name it directly.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
